lesson_title: The Festival That Fills in the Final Week: Population Growth Explained
hook_text: A festival open all year. Almost everyone arrives in the last seven days.
clip_script: Imagine a festival ground with gates open for one full year — and every human who ever had to be seated arrives sometime during that year. January, March, July, October: a thin dribble, a family at a time. By Christmas morning, with the year nearly spent, the ground holds only about ONE billion people. That is everything from the first farming villages to 1804. Then comes the final week. Around the twenty-ninth of December the second billion walks in — 1927. The third arrives on the thirtieth — 1960. And through New Year's Eve the gates simply roar: a fresh billion every few hours — 1974, 1987, 1999, 2011 — eight billion just before midnight, in 2022. So what flung the gates open? Not extra births. Death lost its grip. Food, clean water, vaccines, antibiotics — deaths collapsed while births carried on, and the gap blew the total skyward. Humanity did not speed up its births; it slowed down its funerals. And the ending almost nobody knows: the rush is already fading. The growth rate peaked in the late 1960s and keeps falling — South Africa alone went from six children per woman to about two comma three, by choice. The gates are still busy. The queue outside gets shorter every year.
visual_style: A twelve-month calendar burning down beside an aerial festival ground; empty fields for most of the year, then a torrent of dots through the gates in the final week; billion-counters flashing; a last shot of a thinning queue.
mood: Epic time-lapse with a quiet twist ending.
pacing: Slow, sparse months compressed fast, explosive final-week rush, calm reflective close.
